item.title: Max Verstappen takes pole for Las Vegas Grand Prix after Kimi Antonelli penalty
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Kimi Antonelli was quickest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, but the newly-crowned world champion will not be on pole for Sunday’s race as he has a five-place grid penalty for taking a new engine for this meeting. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, who was second, will take pole – his first in Las Vegas – and Mercedes’ George Russell will line up alongside him on the front row of the grid after finishing in third. Antonelli will start from sixth.

Lando Norris was fourth for McLaren and Isack Hadjar fifth for Red Bull. The Ferrari was not in good shape in Las Vegas however. Lewis Hamilton was struggling with a lack of grip throughout the session and could not hook up a good lap. Neither he nor his teammate Charles Leclerc could make it out of Q2, with Leclerc finishing in 11th and Hamilton in 12th. They will start from 10th and 11th after McLaren’s Oscar Piastri also has a 10-place penalty for taking a new engine.

Having won the title in Mexico, Antonelli had said he wanted to see out the season strongly as he and team look towards 2027 and the 20-year-old Italian was once more in immense form in Las Vegas, even if it did not yield pole. Had he done so it would have been his eighth of the season and second in four races despite the resurgence of Red Bull and with Ferrari and McLaren having been quick in recent rounds.

He and Mercedes will take great heart from having proved once more they are on top of their car and that the recent upgrades are working and prove the correct direction for next year’s model. For three rounds now the Mercedes, in Antonelli’s hands, has looked as strong as it did early in the season and is once more enjoying a slender advantage over their rivals.

With the pole, Verstappen and Red Bull continue a run of good form that will be a huge boost to the team and bodes well for a strong start next season. After their last tranche of upgrades proved so effective, Verstappen has taken pole in three of the last six rounds and won three of the last five. He has form in Nevada with two previous wins here and another cannot be ruled out. Verstappen felt he had extracted the best from his car, even if he was still over two tenths off Antonelli’s time in a car that has been something of a handful for the Dutchman this weekend.

With the low temperatures at night in Las Vegas, warming the tyres was key and the field did build laps to force heat into them, before putting in a quick run. In the first hot runs in Q3 it was clear that working as teammates to deliver a tow was proving hugely beneficial but, although Russell was behind Antonelli for his first effort, he was not close enough for the tow.

Russell did take the top spot with his run but was followed by Verstappen who had been squarely in the slipstream of his teammate Hadjar and the Dutchman went quicker by almost three-tenths. The benefit was clear and the British driver then specifically asked the team if he could have a tow from Antonelli given the Italian had a grid penalty.

There was jostling for position for the final runs with no driver wanting to be at the front of the field. Hadjar ultimately took on the mantle once more, leading out Verstappen but the Dutchman could not improve.

Similarly, Oscar Piastri was delivering a slipstream for Norris but he too could not improve. Russell had no tow from Antonelli who had backed out of the jostling and was ploughing his own furrow at the back. It was a close run thing for the Italian, but in dropping back he crossed the line to start his lap with just one second to spare.

Russell moved up to second but it was the Italian world champion who had kept the best for last, taking the top spot with a time of 1minute 33.893seconds. The slipstream had worked but the quickest man on track would not take pole, leaving Russell perhaps to wonder quite why the team did not favour him on this occasion. He said he would discuss it with Mercedes “offline”.

Verstappen and Russell were investigated by the stewards for an incident where they banged wheels at turn 14 in final practice. Verstappen had overtaken Russell on the way into the corner, and Russell reciprocated by ducking back up the inside and the pair clashed.

Verstappen accused Russell of trying to push him into the barriers, while the British driver’s race engineer Marcus Dudley said he had seen the Dutchman “cut in front of you”. Russell’s described it as “fun and games”. Verstappen was given a warning by the FIA stewards but no penalty.

Source: The Guardian US | Published: 2026-11-21 06:00 UTC

item.title: Campaigners back call for scrutiny of consent laws by Joanne Young
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Campaigners have welcomed a call for scrutiny of consent laws by a survivor of drug-facilitated rape but said action must also focus on wider issues around sexual assault.

Joanne Young, who was drugged and raped by her husband and sexually abused by men he invited into their home, warned of “serious questions about how the law deals with consent”.

Philip Young, 50, advertised Joanne Young, his then wife, on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court heard. In fact, he had been sedating her, plunging her into an “inanimate state” in which anything could be done to her by the men who answered the adverts, jurors were told.

The former Conservative councillor pleaded guilty earlier in the year to dozens of charges of abuse against his former wife, who has waived her right to anonymity.

As four men were convicted of sexual offences against her on Thursday, Young, 49, said: “No one should be able to give [consent] on your behalf.” Her daughter, Alex Young, also called for a change in the law to make it clear that third-party consent cannot ever be used as an argument in a court of law.

Barristers and campaigners said there was no law that stated third-party consent was a valid defence as they called for a public debate and further education about consent.

Kate Parker, a criminal barrister and founder of the charity Schools Consent Project, said: “The law currently has nothing in it which allows someone to point to another person and say: ‘Because of what they told me, I believed the other person to be consenting.’ You can’t effectively outsource consent to a third party, the law has never had that within it. The Sexual Offences Act 2003 certainly doesn’t have that in it.

“What is instead happening is defence counsel in this case, and in cases like this, are pointing to a defence you can run, which is to say that the defendant genuinely and reasonably thought that the victim was consenting.”

The trial heard that the four men, who were strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her. The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.

Parker said it was right that a defendant should be able to say what was in his or her mind at the time of an alleged offence.

“I think that’s a sort of cornerstone of our law. But I hope that these arguments carry less and less traction with juries when generally there is more knowledge as to what the laws around consent are,” she said.

“I hope that as time goes by, juries become more aware and members of the public become more aware as to what the law on consent is, so no one can say: ‘Because a third party told me so and I acted on it, I thought I was legally safe.’”

Harriet Wistrich, a solicitor and the director of the Centre for Women’s Justice, said the jury in the Young case had ultimately rejected the defence.

“It should be obvious in the law that somebody can’t consent on somebody else’s behalf. But you could explicitly make it the case,” she said.

“Defence barristers should robustly defend their clients. That’s their job. But they shouldn’t overstep the mark by relying on myths and stereotypes.”

Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales, agreed the law on consent should be scrutinised. The Sexual Offences Act 2003 states: “A person consents if he agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice.”

She said: “We can look at strengthening existing laws. But really we have to get to the root of the problem, which is about the understanding of consent.

“The existing law is already clear. This is about how that law is interpreted and it is regularly misinterpreted and misapplied. That happens all the time by defendants, by barristers, by juries, and so this is highlighting a lack of understanding that consent is specific: it’s not a one-time event, it’s ongoing, it’s highly dependent on the actual situation at the time. The fact that someone is unconscious necessarily means they can’t consent.

“The other thing about these cases is that drugging someone is the opposite of consent. What is emerging from these organised drug-facilitated sexual abuse cases is a growing recognition of the attraction that some people have to a woman not being able to consent.”

Prof Miranda Horvath, the director of the Institute for Social Justice and Crime at the University of Suffolk, said incorrect beliefs about consent should be “robustly challenged”.

“It is incredibly important that people understand that legally nobody can give consent on your behalf, and this underlines the importance of clear education on consent through society, from young people right through to adults,” she said.

“Rape and serious sexual offences are a direct choice made by perpetrators, and a lack of understanding on whether a sexual partner has given consent cannot be an acceptable excuse.”

The Labour MP Jess Phillips said the government should look at whether the law should be tightened. “It is absolutely right that the government should strength-test whether there is a way of really asserting in the law that consent cannot ever come from a third party – we need to be absolutely satisfied that that is the case,” she said.

“There is an argument that while the law states that consent cannot come from a third party, we still see it being used as a defence. Perhaps if we look at tightening the law, these men would have had to plead guilty and Joanne Young would have been spared this trial.”

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “The law is clear: no one can consent on someone else’s behalf. Consent must come from the person themselves, and they must have the freedom and capacity to make that choice. We keep the criminal law under review, and we will always look at what more can be done to protect victims.”

Source: The Guardian World | Published: 2026-11-21 06:00 UTC

item.title: Can Israel’s opposition bloc stay united against Netanyahu?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Can Israel’s opposition bloc stay united against Netanyahu?

Eisenkot’s fragile alliance must overcome deep ideological divisions to turn its opposition into a government.

As negotiations over the formation of Israel’s next government approach their first deadline of December 6, caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appears to be seeking to exploit divisions within the opposition “change” alliance trying to oust him.

On Wednesday, he held an undeclared meeting with one of its leading figures, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, in a move that has prompted accusations that Netanyahu is attempting to fracture the bloc from within.

The meeting, which lasted two and a half hours, was described by Netanyahu’s office as a “security briefing”. Sources within the opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, however, characterised it as a “strategic disaster”, according to Israeli media.

Bennett had not informed Eisenkot of the meeting in advance, sources told the outlet Ynet. During a subsequent gathering of opposition leaders, Bennett is reported to have argued that they should try to pursue the possibility of a unity government with Netanyahu, Channel 12 reported.

Bennett, a right-winger, is among several prominent figures in the opposition alliance who have previously served in Netanyahu-led governments. Eisenkot himself joined Netanyahu’s emergency unity government following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, serving as a minister without portfolio and a member of the war cabinet.

Avigdor Lieberman, meanwhile – another right-wing member of the opposition bloc – served as Netanyahu’s foreign minister and defence minister.

“Netanyahu is trying to break up the [opposition] bloc for change through Bennett,” a senior figure in the Eisenkot-led alliance told Ynet in an article referencing the numerous pledges by opposition leaders, including Bennett, never to serve within a Netanyahu-led coalition again.

However, given the broad array of ideologies among the coalition leaders, stretching from the hard-right policies of Lieberman to the relatively left-wing platform of Democrats’ leader Yair Golan, and many having previously worked with Netanyahu, it remains unclear how long the bloc can maintain its unity.

Bennett himself was once among Netanyahu’s closest political allies, serving in several of his governments before breaking with him in 2021, when the opportunity arose to form an alternative administration with centrist Yair Lapid. Bennett and Lapid subsequently assembled a cross-party coalition that ended Netanyahu’s 12 consecutive years in office, with Bennett taking the premiership for the first half of its term. But he still shares many policy positions with Netanyahu.

So how cohesive is the opposition coalition, and what could be its potential breaking points?

Here’s what we know:

Is the change bloc united ideologically?

All of the bloc’s members supported Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza – at least at its start – as well as its attacks on several regional states, including Iran and Lebanon.

In terms of domestic policy, however, there are marked differences between members of the alliance.

Both the bloc’s leader, former Israeli military Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, and Bennett’s electoral partner, Yair Lapid, are regarded as relatively centrist figures. By contrast, Bennett and Lieberman are firmly on the right, divided largely by their attitudes towards religion: Bennett is a religious nationalist, while Liberman is a staunchly secular politician with a background in Israel’s Russian-speaking community, increasingly at odds with Israel’s powerful religious political currents.

Standing apart is the left-wing Yair Golan, a supporter of a two-state solution with the Palestinians and an outspoken critic of settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank, which he has accused the government of encouraging or tolerating.

Is the alliance under strain?

Yes.

Beyond the prospect of Netanyahu – Israel’s longest-serving prime minister – continually attempting to undermine them, Eisenkot faces the formidable task of finding the additional 13 seats needed for a parliamentary majority. His bloc holds just 48 of the parliament’s 120 seats after the October 27 elections, leaving him dependent on bridging deep political divides among his allies if he is to form a government capable of governing.

Golan has already met political leaders from parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel and spoken enthusiastically about forming a government with their support. However, that suggestion has been rejected by the rest of the bloc, and has provoked fierce opposition, with right-wing protesters even threatening civil war at the prospect.

Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beytenu party holds seven seats, has been particularly emphatic in rejecting any government dependent on Palestinian support. However, his longstanding and highly vocal opposition to the de facto exemption of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men from military service appears to be softening in the face of another possibility: the 13 seats held by the ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism.

Lieberman’s willingness to compromise on conscription risks undermining one of his central electoral promises, as well as those of other opposition leaders, and could prompt a backlash from supporters.

Have the change bloc’s differences come out in the open?

In August, Bennett dismissed Eisenkot’s proposal to allow limited exemptions from military conscription that would cover the ultra-Orthodox as an “insane mistake”, warning that ultra-Orthodox politicians Aryeh Deri and Moshe Gafni would “run circles around” him. Eisenkot subsequently countered, accusing Bennett and Lieberman of engaging in “old politics” and damaging the opposition’s electoral prospects by refusing to agree that the largest party in the alliance should lead the next government.

Lieberman, just weeks before the election, branded Eisenkot “Gantz 2.0” – referring to former defence minister Benny Gantz, who joined Netanyahu’s government in 2020 despite campaigning against him – accusing Eisenkot of secretly pursuing a deal with Netanyahu and acting out of personal ambition. Golan, meanwhile, told Lieberman several days after the election that, if he was to continue to insist on a government that avoids conscripting ultra-Orthodox men, he was “welcome to form one with Netanyahu”.

What did change bloc leaders say about Netanyahu before entering the opposition?

Their previous assessments of Netanyahu have not always been so harsh.

In 2020, Bennett told reporters that, despite their personal differences, he respected Netanyahu “very much”, adding that Israel had “won a victory” by having him in office for so long and that he had “done great things” for the country.

Lieberman, meanwhile, told The Jerusalem Post in 2019 that he wished Netanyahu “only really good results” and hoped that he would be acquitted on the corruption charges that he has since cited, on numerous occasions, as evidence that the prime minister is unfit for office.

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-21 05:46 UTC

Original link: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/21/can-israels-opposition-bloc-stay-united-against-netanyahu?traffic_source=rss

item.title: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend

- Published

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has labelled Vladimir Putin as a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.

Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".

On the sidelines of a historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin on Thursday, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".

At least nine people were killed in Russian attacks targeting bridges in Kyiv and railway stations on Friday, days after Ukraine badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.

Zelensky called the attack the "biggest this year" and said the country suffered civilian deaths and injuries after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.

Hours after the strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".

"They (Zelensky and Putin) both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.

Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.

However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".

"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he said.

Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he is a "friend" means "he doesn't feel enough pressure".

The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the southeast of the country early on Friday.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said one missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The missile hit about 100km (62 miles) from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the Coalition of the Winning - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said. Another missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.

item.title: ‘So what if there’s a hole? It hasn’t collapsed’: Kyiv residents unbothered by Russian attacks on city’s bridges
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.

Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.

“So what if there’s a hole? The bridge hasn’t collapsed. You need to know a bit about bridge construction,” says Mykola, 65, at the wheel of a half -full afternoon bus as it clatters on its way west.

Mykola operates a marshrutka, a single deck private bus, whose drivers are famed in Kyiv mythology for being able to multi-task: chatting, smoking and collecting fares, while driving as fast as possible to take passengers from rivals.

Passengers pay 25 hryvnia (42p) in cash and typically one passenger gets the unofficial job of taking money and handing back change on behalf of the driver. It turns out this has become the Guardian’s task, in order to conduct an interview.

“It would be very difficult to destroy the bridge. It would take a huge number of missiles, and if one or two hit it, it wouldn’t be the end of the world,” Mykola continues, with behind-the-wheel speculation that is so far accurate. By lunchtime the holes have been covered up, perhaps to avoid unsettling passengers eyeing the Dnipro River below.

Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population.

Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.

As of Friday, in an already traffic-snarled city, Kyiv’s other main road bridge, the Southern Bridge, was allowing motor traffic only from east to west. The new Podilskyi Bridge, damaged early on Friday, was similarly restricted, and the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, told people to avoid car travel after a night in which six were killed.

The Northern Bridge remains open for public transport – plus any cyclists, scooter riders and walkers willing to brave the damp late autumn weather and ignore missile and drone alerts. But below, earthworks have begun to prepare for a floating pontoon bridge, one of eight planned, in case of the worst.

Dmytro Bespalov, a transport planning expert with Kyiv’s National University of Construction and Architecture, said it was difficult to destroy a suspension bridge like the Northern. They have “a strong construction, with a lot of repairability”, meaning damage can usually be fixed. Though there are holes in the roadway, its supporting structures were so far unscathed, he added.

Russia is thought to have been aiming ballistic missiles at the supporting pylon, requiring a precise and difficult to execute attack, though that is what Ukraine did at the culmination of its complex attack on the Kerch road bridge, which was brought down after a Flamingo cruise missile struck its supporting arch.

Yet, Bespalov cautioned that Kyiv was strategically vulnerable if Russia targets the bridges with “dozens or hundreds” of missiles, because the city did not have enough bridges from before the war. “In 2021, Kyiv was in third place in Europe for congestion on the TomTom traffic index,” he said, behind Istanbul and Moscow.

Particular concern is reserved for the pontoon bridge alternative. They can bear less traffic: “It would take 20 pontoon bridges to have half the current capacity,” Bespalov said – and they are far more vulnerable to missile and drone attack. “I don’t think it would be possible to use pontoons during a red [missile] or yellow [drone] alarm” – not least because vehicles could end up in the water.

At the first busy bus stop on the eastern left bank, Nataliya, 40, and Iryna, 39, are happy to make the crossing over the Northern Bridge. They say they have long got used to the difficulties of war: “The main thing is to get through the first 24 hours at home after the initial discomfort, and then we’ll adapt,” said Nataliya, a customer service specialist.

Iryna added: “If we start to despair, that’s exactly what they want. A bridge can be built. The main thing is that when the attack comes, there are no civilians or military personnel around. It’s just concrete, that’s all. They’ll either repair it or come up with something new.”

It is a core attitude of Kyiv’s remaining residents, who are already contending with hours of electricity shortages and a lack of heating, with the full chill of winter yet to arrive. People want to deal with problems as they arise rather than worrying excessively about what may come – though it is not always easy amid the daily attacks, including a daytime raid on Thursday in which a drone exploded near the Dutch embassy.

Oleksandr, 42, a construction worker, was waiting to get across the bridge. “If the bridges are destroyed we’ll have to leave,” he conceded. If that happened, he and his wife would move to her parents’ house across the river. “I bought them a generator there; they have their own water well. We’d already dug the well during the war. They used to have gas heating, but we’ve converted it to wood-burning. We’re preparing,” he said.

Additional reporting by Galya Rudyk

Source: The Guardian World | Published: 2026-11-21 05:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/21/kyiv-russian-attacks-bridges
